column2: Why? GPIO 39 is input-only and has no internal pull-up resistor, so we add 10 kΩ to 3.3 V. When not pressed the pin reads HIGH; when pressed, the pin connects to GND and reads LOW. For the finished robot, the button moves to breadboard 2 on floor 3 so it is easy to press, connected by two wires to columns 27 and 29 (lengths in Part 6).

Not yet The 6 mm button is only for testing: in Part 6 Step 3 it is removed, then plugged in again on breadboard 2 on floor 3. The bench GND wire (WAGO − to pin G) is also only for testing: on the robot the shared GND comes from the black wire of LM2596 #1 to the 30P board.
STOP button on breadboard 2 → columns 27 and 29 of breadboard 1

Floor 3 (third plate): the S3 board at the rear end with its USB-C port facing sideways, breadboard 2 across in front of it (MAX98357A and INMP441 here), the TFT lying flat facing up in front of it, the pan-tilt head with the ESP32-CAM at the front end, the box speaker standing on the right side, and the STOP button plugged into breadboard 2.
Remove the 6 mm button from breadboard 1 (it will be plugged into breadboard 2 on floor 3). The 10 kΩ pull-up resistor stays where it is.
Tactile button (the 6 mm one from testing, or 12x12 mm)

STOP button on breadboard 2: plug the tactile button across the middle gap in empty columns, near the left edge so it is easy to press. Push until its legs are fully in. Attach two 20 cm (no. 28) jumper wires to two diagonal legs, one on each side of the gap. Do not connect the button legs to the red or blue rails of breadboard 2, or to S3 pins: this button belongs to the body on floor 2.
